query: What signals suggest an incident resolution will be inefficient?

per_column.name: incident_type
per_column.rationale: Categorizing incidents (printer, hardware, software, connectivity) gives a genuine grouping axis to compare resolution efficiency across types. Values are soundly extracted from short_description (e.g. 'Printer not working' -> printer, 'Internet connectivity lost' -> connectivity).

per_column.name: description_clarity
per_column.rationale: Vague descriptions plausibly correlate with inefficient resolution, giving analytical leverage. Values are inferable from text terseness, though the boundary is somewhat subjective; 'Printer not working properly' being False is a defensible reading. Slight subjectivity lowers groundedness modestly.

per_column.name: upstream_dependency
per_column.rationale: Whether an incident depends on upstream systems is a relevant efficiency signal (dependencies delay resolution). 'Unable to connect to the database' -> True is a warranted inference; most rows False is reasonable. Some inference risk but generally grounded in the description text.

per_column.name: problem_recurrence
per_column.rationale: Recurrence is potentially useful for efficiency analysis, but the value 'recurring_device_type' appears to be assigned merely because the incident is a printer/common device type, not from evidence of actual recurrence in the source text. This conflates category with recurrence and asserts recurrence the text does not directly support, weakening groundedness.

judge.rationale: The added columns provide meaningful new axes (type, clarity, dependency, recurrence) for analyzing resolution inefficiency, going beyond the raw ITSM fields. Most values are soundly read from short_description. The main concern is problem_recurrence, which seems to infer recurrence from device commonality rather than actual textual evidence of repeat issues, introducing mild hallucination. Overall the set meets both necessary conditions reasonably well.
